questions.prompt: Why are purchase success, verified evidence, finished delivery and current entitlement different facts?
questions.scenario: A synthetic permanent theme was unlocked. It was later refunded on another device while this installation stayed offline.
questions.androidBridge: Compare Play Billing purchase processing and acknowledgment, but distinguish StoreKit VerificationResult, finish, and entitlement sequences rather than equating APIs.
rubric: Separates verified and unverified evidence and refuses an unverified grant.
Makes delivery recoverable before finish rather than trusting UI success.
Processes revocation for a known transaction and reconciles current entitlement.
Separates authenticity of offline evidence from freshness about remote changes.
Uses different policies for permanent products, consumables and subscriptions.
questions.answerHTML: A successful purchase result still contains a verification result to inspect. Like checking a receipt before handing over goods, the app must accept only verified evidence before granting a right. Finish tells StoreKit that delivery processing is complete. Save a recoverable fulfillment effect before calling finish. Current entitlement means the right the user has now under this product’s rules. Derive it from verified evidence; a purchase-screen Boolean cannot keep it current. A refund can change facts relevant to the same transaction identity, so a seen-ID filter must not discard all subsequent revocation evidence. For the permanent theme, reconcile known verified transactions that have not been revoked. A long-lived owner listens for transaction updates. Offline signed evidence can authenticate a known purchase while failing to reveal a refund that happened remotely after disconnection. Define that freshness policy and explain it to support. A consumable requires an independently durable credit ledger; a subscription needs status and expiration/grace policy. Android acknowledgment experience helps with replay discipline, but is not an exact substitute for StoreKit's verification, finish and entitlement contracts. The synthetic model injects verification and proves none of the actual signature or sandbox behavior.
followUps: Who owns the transaction-update listener, and when is it cancelled on owner change?
How does the policy change for consumable credits or a subscription in billing retry?
pitfalls: Treating successful refund submission as proof that revocation was approved.
Keeping one permanent purchased Boolean or discarding every later update for a known transaction ID.

questions.prompt: How would you recover a stale parcel Live Activity after logout and reject a delayed push from the old account?
questions.scenario: The parcel event remains active while its Live Activity becomes stale and is later dismissed. An old-account update arrives afterward.
questions.androidBridge: Use Android widget/ongoing-notification ownership as an analogy; ActivityKit has distinct system surfaces, lifetime and push update semantics.
rubric: Separates the parcel event, entitlement and visible-surface owners.
Uses an owner generation and domain revision to reject obsolete app updates.
Distinguishes stale, ended and dismissed states.
Reconciles on relaunch and handles disabled or dismissed activities.
Names APNs and device evidence, a simpler alternative and a recovery owner.
questions.answerHTML: Keep the parcel record as the source of truth. The Live Activity shows only a privacy-safe summary derived from it. Logout changes the owner generation, an attempt label that rejects completions from the old owner. A domain revision can reject older parcel facts, but it cannot force APNs delivery order or resurrect an activity the system ended or the person dismissed. Stale content means the estimate is old; it does not mean the parcel completed. Ending supplies a final state with an explicit dismissal policy. On relaunch, inspect the currently tracked activities and current parcel owner. A saved activity ID does not prove that its surface is still active. If Live Activities are disabled or the activity was dismissed, preserve the ordinary in-app parcel task. Compare a regular widget or in-app status for use cases without a meaningful bounded event. Assign mobile surface recovery and server push/token ownership separately. Host policy checks cover owner and lifetime rejection; simulator rendering, device dismissal and APNs token/update behavior remain distinct evidence. Document what is still pending instead of inferring successful integration from an immutable state model.
followUps: Which useful final information is safe to show on the surface after logout?
What evidence separates stale server facts from delayed push delivery?
pitfalls: Promising an always-running extension or exact push-update timing.
Treating a visible Live Activity as authority for paid rights or parcel completion.

questions.prompt: How would you resolve serverRecordChanged while preserving both devices’ offline edits?
questions.scenario: The base has title Draft and note Blue. Local changes title to A; the server changes note to Green. In a second case, the server also changes title to B.
questions.androidBridge: Room gives local transaction consistency; CloudKit change tags and base/local/server conflict policy add remote concurrency that Room alone does not solve.
rubric: Treats the change tag as opaque version evidence and uses a conditional save.
Produces title A and note Green for the separate-field edits.
Keeps local A versus server B as an unresolved title conflict.
Keeps base and local work while building the next attempt from current server system fields.
Bounds retry and preserves a recoverable local draft.
questions.answerHTML: The change tag says which server version the edit was based on. A mismatch correctly stops an overwrite based on an older version. Retain the attempted local record, fetch or use the error's current server record, and compare both with the last synchronized base. This is a three-way comparison: what was shared, what changed here and what changed there. In the first scenario, only local title changed and only server note changed, so the resolved proposal is title A and note Green. Build the next save using the current server version and system fields rather than a guessed tag. In the second case, both devices changed the same title: local A and server B each differ from the shared Draft. That is an unresolved title conflict; preserve both candidates and the base for a user or declared domain decision. A later device timestamp is not enough reason to discard one person’s edit. Another writer may change the server again before retry, so bound retry and retain the local draft on failure. Missing fields and deletion need separate semantic rules. Room's transaction boundary is a useful local analogy, but does not provide this remote conflict policy or establish that a real CloudKit container was tested.
followUps: What separate rule is needed when one device deletes and the other edits?
What must be saved locally before reporting an offline edit as accepted?
pitfalls: Sorting a CloudKit change tag as though it were a timestamp.
Building a replacement from business fields while dropping required server system fields.

questions.prompt: Would you choose a coordinated local document or CloudKit record sync for these cross-device drafts? Explain compatibility, recovery and alternatives.
questions.scenario: The feature needs offline edits, external document-provider access, older-client compatibility and retries after lost acknowledgments.
questions.androidBridge: Compare a Room/outbox plus Android document-provider workflow; Apple's document coordination, iCloud identity and schema evolution are separate mechanisms.
rubric: Separates whole-document access coordination from deciding between conflicting field edits.
Defines stable operation and record identities and an atomic effect-and-receipt boundary.
Fetches after missed notifications and atomically applies changes with their checkpoint.
Handles account generation and additive production schema compatibility.
Names alternatives, evidence owners, rollback and service behavior still unverified.
questions.answerHTML: Ask what users share: a whole document, or individual fields kept synchronized. That determines which model fits the task. A coordinated local document can provide external access and offline editing without promising cloud collaboration; coordination orders cooperating access to the file. It does not decide which old edit should win a business conflict. CloudKit records can provide conditional server saves, with explicit base/local/server merge and account scope. Core Data mirroring is another option when that store owns the model. Either design must keep drafts recoverable and keep the same identity when retrying the same operation. A stable record replacement differs from an exactly-once increment; effect and receipt need the authoritative atomic boundary. Treat CloudKit subscriptions as hints to fetch changes. Recover after missed notifications, and save applied changes together with their checkpoint token. Rotate local owner generation on identity changes. Production CloudKit schema evolution needs older-client compatibility and additive field/index planning. Assign document-provider testing and two-installation cloud conflict testing to separate owners, with a manual export alternative and reversal path. Host reconstruction verifies policy only; it does not prove disk crash safety, signed container access or production schema behavior.
followUps: Which user requirement would make local export the better first version?
How can an expired change token be recovered without erasing pending edits?
pitfalls: Calling atomic file replacement a merge or a complete interprocess transaction.
Adding a custom sync engine over mirrored Core Data objects without defining which system owns synchronization.

questions.prompt: How would you replace the selected emoji in A👩🏽‍💻éB safely, convert its range and register undo while respecting composition and current revision?
questions.scenario: The user selects the emoji. An async validation result arrives while an input method editor, or IME, is still composing text.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java String length uses UTF-16; Swift String indices and Character iteration have different semantics, while both platforms require composition-aware editing.
rubric: Constructs and converts the selection using the correct UTF-16 representation.
Checks whole-Character endpoints and the current document revision separately.
Defers whole-buffer normalization while marked text is active.
Keeps before and after selection and registers one semantic undo and redo.
Rejects obsolete async validation before changing UI text or selection.
questions.answerHTML: One displayed emoji can contain several Unicode pieces. Find its selection using the current Swift Character indices, then convert with NSRange(_:in:) for the UTF-16 API. For a custom whole-Character command, convert the incoming range back and verify both endpoints are Character boundaries; conversion alone does not prove the command selected whole Characters. Replace the entire selection with X, leaving the combining accent attached to its adjacent e. A range from an older document revision can be valid yet semantically wrong, so validate revision before applying it. Save both the text and selection before and after the edit. Undo must restore the intended editing state, not only the characters. For this literal replacement, the resulting caret offset is the validated UTF-16 start plus the replacement's UTF-16 length. Register one semantic reversal and its redo, avoiding duplicate registration for an edit already owned by UITextView. The markedTextRange property identifies text still being composed by the input method. While it exists, do not rewrite that provisional input as if it were committed. Discard the outdated validator result before attribute or selection mutation. Host Foundation checks can test ranges; they do not prove IME, VoiceOver or native undo interaction. Java/Kotlin UTF-16 knowledge helps, but integer offsets are not Swift String subscripts.
followUps: How must the range change if normalization alters text before the selection?
Why can reading a legacy layoutManager affect a TextKit 2 text view?
pitfalls: Treating Swift Character count as UTF-16 NSRange length.
Replacing the entire buffer on every SwiftUI bridge update and disrupting active composition.

questions.prompt: The editor animates a classifier result beside a bundled clip. Which performance branch would you investigate before choosing Metal?
questions.scenario: The proposed fix is Metal, but no trace separates text layout, media preparation, inference and composition cost.
questions.androidBridge: Media3 and Android render-thread experience suggest pipeline boundaries; Apple AVFoundation, Core Animation, Metal and Core ML still require their own evidence.
rubric: Defines end-to-end intervals and a named bottleneck hypothesis.
Separates media loading and decoding, layout and composition, and ML preprocessing and prediction.
Requires selection, output and accuracy checks before a speed claim.
Bounds work and explains why UI-thread GPU waits remove CPU/GPU overlap.
Names a simpler alternative, evidence owner and rollback condition.
questions.answerHTML: Animation alone does not identify the slow stage. First find which work misses the intended interaction deadline. Establish a reproducible interaction, representative device and intervals for clip loading/readiness, text editing/layout, preprocessing, prediction, postprocessing and visible result. Check selection, expected clip behavior and classifier output against known correct results. Those checks are the correctness oracles. A measured decode delay points toward media preparation; a composition hitch points toward layer/layout work; a validated GPU workload may justify Metal. Core Animation already supports ordinary geometry and opacity changes. Compare that simpler path before adding a custom renderer. Metal introduces pipelines, command buffers, resource lifetime and numerical/visual validation; waitUntilCompleted in a UI frame blocks the intended CPU/GPU overlap. Core ML compute-unit configuration also does not guarantee every operation runs on a particular accelerator. Limit queued and running preparation and predictions. Obsolete work must not exhaust memory or publish an old result. Assign the selected interval investigation to an owner and keep simpler playback/layer behavior as a rollback. Source inspection creates hypotheses; physical-device traces and unchanged correctness are required before claiming an optimization. Audio DSP, shader correctness and model evaluation remain separate specialist work.
followUps: How would a first, cold model load change the workload and comparison?
What must an audio render callback avoid, and why is sending work to an arbitrary queue insufficient?
pitfalls: Calling source inspection a measured speedup.
Increasing prediction concurrency without checking memory, accuracy and old-result rejection.

questions.prompt: Why is one granted Boolean insufficient for watch transport, Bluetooth readiness and HealthKit reads?
questions.scenario: The watch is unreachable, Bluetooth is powered off and a health query returns no records after the authorization-request callback succeeds.
questions.androidBridge: Android/Wear permission and transport concepts are useful analogies; HealthKit intentionally hides read grants and WCSession reachability is not authorization.
rubric: Separates availability, product opt-in, system authorization, execution and readiness.
Explains pending watch commands and recovery separately from replacing the latest snapshot.
Separates Bluetooth power, discovery, connection and validated payload.
Keeps HealthKit read permission ambiguous and explains saving-status semantics.
Offers a usable fallback without repeated coercive permission prompts.
questions.answerHTML: Permission, reachability and usable data answer different questions. One granted flag cannot preserve those answers. A watch counterpart can be installed and activated yet unreachable for an immediate message; a command with a stable ID can wait in the queue. Latest-state context instead replaces the previous snapshot. These delivery models are different. Bluetooth authorization can coexist with powered-off hardware, and a connected peripheral still needs discovered characteristics and validated payloads before its reading is useful. HealthKit deliberately hides whether read access was granted. That privacy rule limits what the app can infer. Authorization request success does not mean all requested types were granted, and empty read results do not reveal denial. The authorizationStatus(for:) method describes permission to save that type, not permission to read it. Present no visible data with a manual path rather than inventing a read-denied state. Product opt-in is yet another input, distinct from system grants. A shared wrapper may expose service-specific values, but must preserve these distinctions instead of flattening them into granted. Host feature selection injects the facts and invokes none of the native services. Wear OS and Android permission experience helps ask the questions, but cannot override Apple's read-visibility or transport semantics.
followUps: Which owner generation should reject an old-account Bluetooth notification?
What truthful message and manual fallback should be shown when health data is empty for an unknown reason?
pitfalls: Treating a successful HealthKit request callback as a read-permission grant.
Treating Bluetooth authorization as proof that hardware is on or the received data is authenticated.

questions.prompt: Choose one watch, spatial, accessory or health feature for the checklist. How would you verify adoption and safely reverse the choice?
questions.scenario: The small team can support one elective feature. The checklist must remain usable when capability, consent or execution becomes unavailable.
questions.androidBridge: Wear OS feature selection and optional Android capabilities inform the decision; Apple targets, system spatial input and background limits are independently validated.
rubric: Chooses one concrete user task and compares a simpler alternative.
Names owners, data authority, input or transport contract and fallback.
Separates simulator layout checks from paired-device, hardware and comfort evidence.
Defines account, replay and privacy recovery with staged adoption.
Sets observable stop or reversal criteria without inventing benefits.
questions.answerHTML: One option is a watch Mark packed action: a small task useful without taking out the phone. Compare it with the existing phone checklist, then define latest snapshot context separately from queued commands. The source-of-truth store applies the operation ID and account generation together with a receipt, atomically. The watch UI owns the pending display and recovery when that reply is lost. Unsupported or opted-out users retain the phone task. Name the phone/watch protocol owner and the support owner. Observe delivery and failure on paired devices before promoting adoption. A simulator can check layout but not transport budgets. If choosing visionOS instead, begin with a window and system controls, which support indirect selection without exposing raw gaze; hardware comfort is separate evidence. Bluetooth needs protocol/device validation, and HealthKit needs type-scoped purpose plus ambiguous-read UX. Introduce the feature in stages under an explicit product decision. Reverse or stop if pending actions remain confusing or support burden is unacceptable. No assumed benefit, course attendance or host success establishes user adoption or a full platform integration.
followUps: Which observed user or support outcome would favor keeping the phone-only feature?
How would platform-specific checks prevent a shared package from exposing unsupported APIs?
pitfalls: Adding every named framework merely to claim platform breadth.
Treating background modes, workout sessions or immersive entry as permanent permission to execute.
